faq.q: Why is methacholine preferred over histamine for AHR testing?

exam: What is the most appropriate next step in a 7‑year‑old with intermittent wheeze and normal spirometry? — Perform a methacholine challenge to confirm AHR; if unavailable, trial of inhaled corticosteroid and observe response.

A patient with chronic cough and wheeze improves only with systemic steroids. What does this suggest? — Likely a steroid‑responsive inflammatory airway disease such as asthma or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis; consider long‑term inhaled steroid.

You are in a rural clinic with no spirometer. A child presents with wheeze after a cold. How would you assess AHR? — Use peak flow monitoring and observe variability; if >20% between readings, AHR is likely.
A patient on β2‑agonist inhaler reports no relief. What is the most likely explanation? — Poor inhaler technique or incorrect device; review technique and consider spacer.
Why is systemic corticosteroid avoided in uncomplicated asthma exacerbations? — It has significant systemic side effects and is not needed when a SABA provides adequate bronchodilation.
Which trigger is most common in East African households that contributes to AHR? — Indoor biomass smoke from cooking fires; advise improved ventilation or cleaner fuels.
ai.title: Airway Hyperresponsiveness
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A functional abnormality of the lower airways where bronchial smooth muscle contracts excessively to non‑specific stimuli, causing airflow limitation. It is the hallmark of asthma and can be triggered by infections, allergens, irritants or systemic disease.

b: AHR is not a disease but a pathophysiological state.
It is present in most asthma phenotypes but can also occur in COPD and post‑viral bronchiolitis.
sections.p: Airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) is a heightened bronchial response to various stimuli, measured by a fall in FEV1 or peak flow after a provocation test. It is a key diagnostic criterion for asthma.

t.b: Does the patient have AHR? A PC20 (concentration causing 20% fall in FEV1) ≤ 8 µg/mL confirms AHR.
Same principle as methacholine; used where methacholine is unavailable.

b: Step 1: Intermittent symptoms, normal spirometry.
Step 2: Mild persistent, FEV1 >80% predicted.
Step 3: Moderate, FEV1 60–80% predicted.
Step 4: Severe, FEV1 40–60% predicted.
Step 5: Very severe, FEV1 <40% predicted or frequent exacerbations.
sections.p: Severity is graded by the degree of reversible airflow limitation and symptom burden, using the Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) steps.

b: Acute viral bronchiolitis or pneumonia in children.
Chronic exposure to biomass smoke, indoor cooking fires.
HIV infection with opportunistic respiratory infections.
Tuberculosis with post‑TB bronchiectasis.
Sickle cell disease causing repeated pulmonary crises.
Schistosomiasis with pulmonary involvement.
Use of herbal remedies containing irritants.
Occupational dusts in mining or textile work.
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, infections and environmental exposures dominate.

b: Wheeze is typically expiratory, audible in the chest and may be absent during attacks.
Cough may be dry or productive, especially in infections.
Exercise or cold air precipitates symptoms.
Symptoms improve with bronchodilators.
sections.p: Patients present with episodic wheeze, cough, chest tightness and dyspnoea, often worse at night or early morning.
Investigations aim to confirm reversible obstruction and exclude mimics.

t.b: Rule out pneumonia, pneumothorax or mass lesions.

b: Stridor or inspiratory wheeze indicates upper airway involvement.
Rapidly worsening hypoxia or cyanosis.
Severe hypotension or altered mental status.
sections.p: Urgent care is needed if there is impending respiratory failure or systemic signs of infection.

b: Short‑acting β2‑agonists (SABA) for acute relief – chosen for rapid onset and low systemic toxicity.
Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) for long‑term control – reduce airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness.
Leukotriene receptor antagonists in patients with allergic rhinitis or aspirin sensitivity.
Avoid systemic steroids unless severe exacerbation or steroid‑responsive infection.
Consider anticholinergics in patients with chronic cough or COPD overlap.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide bronchodilation, and control inflammation.

b: Teach patients to recognise early symptoms and use rescue inhaler.
Advise on reducing indoor smoke exposure and improving ventilation.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus.
Screen for HIV and TB in high‑prevalence areas.
sections.p: Regular review of inhaler technique, adherence and trigger avoidance is essential.

b: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease – fixed obstruction, less reversible.
Bronchiectasis – productive cough, often with infection.
Pulmonary embolism – sudden dyspnoea but no wheeze.
Heart failure – orthopnoea and crackles, not wheeze.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic AHR but lack reversible obstruction.

b: Spirometry can be normal in mild intermittent asthma.
Peak flow variability may be low in patients with poor adherence.
Methacholine challenge may be unavailable, leading to diagnostic delay.
sections.p: Certain tests may appear normal despite AHR.
